unit.title: Algebra Synthesis and Precalculus Readiness
unit.act: Finale - Choosing structure instead of chapter labels
unit.role: Turn accumulated techniques into independent classification, strategy, checking, and modeling.
unit.governingQuestion: When the problem is unlabeled, how do we decide what structure it has and what method applies?
unit.storyArc: Students classify objects and equation families, choose transformations, track implications and restrictions, use technology responsibly, and complete a sustained model that coordinates words, pictures, graphs, and symbols.
outcomes: Classify mathematical objects and equation families.
Track restrictions, candidates, and extraneous solutions.
Decide between exact, approximate, algebraic, and graphical answers.
Complete a sustained Precalculus-readiness modeling argument.
unit.investigation: A final modeling capstone requiring variable definition, diagram, model selection, solution, restrictions, units, graph, sensitivity, and written conclusion.
unit.mastery: Readiness requires success across symbolic fluency, representations, explanation, and modeling; a hidden prerequisite failure routes to targeted review.

lessons.title: Classifying mathematical objects
lessons.outcome: Identify whether a prompt contains an expression, equation, inequality, system, or function and determine the requested action.

opening.prompt: Sort a mixed collection of unlabeled tasks.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make classifying mathematical objects necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.

exposition: Identify whether a prompt contains an expression, equation, inequality, system, or function and determine the requested action. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In classifying mathematical objects, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Object sorting board. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Structure tree. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.
